title: Escape analysis: why that variable ended up on the heap

videos.script: Go has no keyword that puts a value on the heap. You write the same code either way, and the compiler decides where each value lives. {{ask}} This lesson asks it. One flag, gcflags equals minus m, makes the compiler print its decisions. What stays on the stack, what moves to the heap, and, with minus m equals two, the reason. {{cases}} Then the reasons, one small program each. A pointer that is returned. A number put in an interface. A closure, a map key, a method value. An array too big for the stack, and a slice whose size arrives at run time. {{inline}} Then the inliner, which can change the answer without a line of yours changing. One directive flips it. {{cost}} Then the price, measured. A benchmark runs the same function with and without the escape, and counts the nanoseconds and the bytes. {{hits}} Last, hits. Every line it reads costs one allocation, and the compiler says why. Remove that reason and it names another. Sometimes the honest result is that an escape is necessary, and the report tells you that too.
